title: adaptive-kernel-queueing-lab-notes-2029-01-15
content:
Purpose and context:
This note collects the lab week work for the adaptive kernel queueing spike (Jan 8–15, 2029). The goal of the spike is to reduce 95th/99th token-latency tails on short-session traffic without regressions to median latency or token throughput. We are exploring: 1) small-window adaptive queueing (AQ) that varies dispatch thresholds based on recent latency feedback, 2) KV-cache prioritization for hot prefixes, and 3) a minimally invasive kernel handshake change to avoid wakeups on tiny batches.

What we ran this week (experiments):
- AQ-v1: baseline adaptive-queueing with window=200ms, min-batch=4, max-wait=25ms. Deployed to shadow traffic on canary1.
- AQ-v2-backpressure: same as v1 but with soft backpressure that reduces accept-rate when qlen>512. Deployed to canary2.
- KV-hotmark: small heuristic that tags prefixes seen > N times in the last T=60s and pins them to prioritized prefill lanes. Applied in local cluster and canary2.
- Kernel-handshake-opt: change to kernel scheduling that defers expensive thread wakeups for sub-8-token batches. Benchmarked in lab nodes only. PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/5890.

Quick results summary (raw observations):
- AQ-v1 reduced median dispatch latency by ~6% on short sessions, 95th by 12% in the shadow traces, but increased CPU busy loop time by ~3% in some kernels.
- AQ-v2-backpressure avoided CPU busy time spikes when load ramped but introduced an occasional 250ms queue-surge on a pathological burst pattern (rare traffic shape).
- KV-hotmark cut token generation latency for a small subset (~2% of requests) by ~20% because prefill avoided recurrent KV lookups. However it slightly increased memory churn in the prefill lanes; eviction needed tuning.
- Kernel-handshake-opt increased end-to-end token latency for mid-size batches (12–30 tokens) by ~4% due to delayed thread wakeups, but reduced tail JIT/thermal spikes during sustained micro-batch traffic.

Logs and notable incidents:
- Jan 12 09:43 — Canary2 observed a short-lived queue surge (250ms) correlated to AQ-v2-backpressure + large burst from partner test harness. Root cause: simultaneous backpressure throttling at ingress + sudden arrival spike that bypassed the admission heuristic. Mitigation: throttle admission smoothing (see action A2).
- Jan 13 14:18 — KV-hotmark caused prefill lane memory high-water at 78% on a node due to hot prefixes from a test dataset; auto-eviction did not trigger because prefix score TTL not decayed. Fixed TTL config in staging (Priya).
- Jan 14 21:02 — Kernel-handshake-opt trial node recorded lower thermal oscillation on sustained 90% GPU utilization runs. Noted that kernel scheduling reduced scheduler wakeups by ~18% in the trace.

Metrics snapshot (shadow traces vs baseline):
- median token dispatch latency: baseline 12.4ms -> AQ-v1 11.6ms -> AQ-v2 11.9ms
- 95th token dispatch latency: baseline 32ms -> AQ-v1 28ms -> AQ-v2 27.5ms (except surge windows)
- CPU scheduler busy delta: +3% (AQ-v1), +1% (AQ-v2 post-backpressure tweak)
- KV-prefill hit rate: baseline 4% -> KV-hotmark 6.2% for targeted prefixes

Decisions made this week:
- Keep AQ approach but move to a hybrid admission policy: adaptive-wait + stochastic early-release for very low-latency requests. This aims to keep medians low without burning cycles. (Decision owner: Aisha)
- Don’t flip kernel-handshake-opt into broad canary yet; needs a follow-up micro-benchmark against mid-batch workloads. Will test parametrized wake-delay. (Owner: Lin)
- Promote KV-hotmark to extended shadow with stricter eviction and TTL decay (Owner: Priya).

Open questions / unresolved:
- How does AQ interact with multi-tenant routing when one tenant sends tiny bursts while another sends long sessions? Do we need tenant-aware admission?
- Is the occasional 250ms surge acceptable if very rare vs. guaranteed lower 95th overall? We need SRE/ops risk thresholds.
- What's the right telemetry to detect dangerous prefill-memory regimes before OOM? Current mem alarms are too coarse.

Action items and owners (short):
- A1: Implement admission-smoothing (sliding-average of accept-rate) for AQ-v2 to prevent synchronized backpressure. Target PR + bench by Jan 22. Owner: Diego.
- A2: Add tenant-weighted admission experiment to simulate one noisy tenant. Create synthetic workload in lab. Owner: Samir (due Jan 24).
- A3: KV-hotmark eviction tuning: add TTL decay and tail-weighted eviction priority; run memory regression test. Owner: Priya (due Jan 18).
- A4: Kernel-handshake micro-bench harness: parameter sweep for wake-delay and measure mid-batch regressions. Owner: Lin (due Jan 20).
- A5: SRE sync to align acceptable surge windows and alert thresholds; include sample traces from Jan 12 incident. Owner: Aisha (schedule meeting Jan 19).

Notes to self / ideas for next spike:
- Explore a tiny-user fastlane: a separate dispatch path for requests < X tokens that enforces a very small batching window (3–6ms) and aggressive prefetching of KV; worth an A/B as it targets worst tails for chat UX.
- Consider a cheap hardware-assist heuristic: use GPU-smoothed utilization signal to lower AQ window when thermal headroom drops.
- Audit all metrics names: ensure we can slice latency by "admission-path" (e.g., fastlane|regular|backpressure).

Appendix: quick checklist for canary rollout when we converge:
- [ ] Perf synthetic run across 10k user-mix sessions
- [ ] Add smoke test that reproduces Jan12 surge pattern
- [ ] Gradual ramp: 0.5% -> 2% -> 10% -> 50% with rollback hooks
- [ ] Add prefill-memory early-warning alarm (node-level 65% prefill mem)
- [ ] Post-launch 24h replay analysis for tail regressions

Slack threads and PRs to review:
- thread: #serving-runtime-ops "AQ backlog + surge" (Jan12)
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/5890 (kernel-handshake-opt)
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/5897 (kv-hotmark prototype)

If you want a shorter summary for exec / PM:
- 1-line: Adaptive queueing + smart KV prioritization reduced 95th token latency on short sessions by ~12% in early shadows; we hit a rare surge pattern and memory bumpable for hot prefixes — plan is to refine admission smoothing, tune prefill eviction, and run more micro-benchmarks before wider canary.

Notes: some sections are intentionally rough — this is a lab-week working note rather than a launch brief. Ping me (Aisha) for clarifications or to see raw traces.
